name: African hair threading

lead: African hair threading wraps sections of hair tightly in wool, cotton or nylon thread to create patterned styles. It is a protective style, helping prevent breakage, and it is also used to elongate tightly coiled hair without heat.
The result is a stretched or sculpted hairstyle that lasts until the threads are removed. It is documented as a centuries-old tradition, especially in West and Central Africa.

paras: Hair is divided into sections and each is wrapped along its length with thread and secured; variations include corkscrew (spiral) wraps and flat twists, and contrasting thread colours can accent patterns. The thread is later unwound, often leaving stretched hair.
Wrapping very tightly can pull on the scalp and edges; tension-related hair loss (traction alopecia) is a general risk of tight styles.

angle.text: Threading shapes natural hair into patterned styles and holds it stretched without heat. Practitioners also use it as a protective style that reduces breakage.

lead: African hair threading, also called threading, is a traditional technique from sub-Saharan Africa in which sections of hair are wrapped with thread, typically wool, cotton or nylon, to form patterns.[1] It is reported to date back to at least the 15th century and is especially prevalent in West and Central Africa.[1]

It has regional names: isi owu among the Igbo, Irun Kiko in Yoruba, Akweley Waabii among the Ga in Ghana and Nywele in Swahili.[1] Wikipedia describes it as a protective style that helps prevent breakage.[1]
People use it to style and stretch natural hair; the corkscrew style gives springy sections and flat twists are another variation.[1] No clinical studies on threading were found.

paras: Hair is parted into sections and each section is wrapped with thread and secured firmly.[1] Style depends on hair pattern and on section shape, size and direction; contrasting thread colours highlight patterns.[1]
The practice is said to go back centuries.[1] Named variants include Ghana's "Adonko" style, also called "Watchman's Wife".[1]
In hair-care discussions, threading appears as a heat-free way to stretch coily hair before styling and as a protective style.
